questions.question: 16. CF patient with 3 weeks of therapy with worsening FEV1. Fungus grows on day 3. Sputum shows the following:

parts.text: What is the organism (genus and species)
What is the syndrome
Name 4 diagnostic features
For treatment, what is first line
What is another treatment you could do

questions.model_answer:
a) Organism: Aspergillus fumigatus.
b) Syndrome: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA).
c) 4 diagnostic features: (1) markedly elevated total serum IgE (>1000 IU/mL); (2) elevated Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE and/or positive immediate skin test reactivity to Aspergillus; (3) peripheral blood eosinophilia; (4) central bronchiectasis and/or pulmonary infiltrates on chest CT (elevated Aspergillus-specific IgG is also an accepted feature).
d) First-line treatment: oral corticosteroids (prednisone).
e) Another treatment option: itraconazole (azole antifungal, used as a steroid-sparing agent).

questions.question: 19yo F with CF not improving on usual therapy. Mold grows from cultures.

parts.text: What is the clinical syndrome
What is the causative agent
What are 4 diagnostic criteria for this syndrome
What is the treatment
What is a second agent to add to therapy

questions.model_answer:
a) Clinical syndrome: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA).
b) Causative agent: Aspergillus fumigatus.
c) 4 diagnostic criteria: (1) markedly elevated total serum IgE (>1000 IU/mL); (2) elevated Aspergillus-specific IgE and/or positive immediate skin test reactivity; (3) peripheral eosinophilia; (4) new/worsening central bronchiectasis or pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging (elevated Aspergillus-specific IgG is also acceptable).
d) Treatment: oral corticosteroids (prednisone).
e) Second agent to add: itraconazole (steroid-sparing azole antifungal).

questions.question: CF patient has progressively worse lung function and symptoms not responsive to IV therapy. Sputum shows a mould at 3 days.

parts.text: What is the organism?
What is the diagnosis?
What are 4 diagnostic criteria?
What is one recommended treatment and one adjunct?

cohort_answer.text: Organism: Aspergillus fumigatus. Diagnosis: most likely allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) - chronic aspergillosis does not quite fit based on diagnostic criteria. Diagnostic criteria: Predisposing condition (asthma or CF); Increased Aspergillus IgE or Type I hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus skin test; Increased Total IgE (>1000 IU/mL); at least 2 of: increased IgG to aspergillus, radiographic pulmonary opacities consistent with ABPA, eosinophilia >500 cells/uL in steroid-naive patients. Treatment: Systemic glucocorticoids are mainstay (e.g. prednisone 0.5 mg/kg daily x14 days, then every-other-day 0.5mg/kg, taper/discontinue at 3 months; total serum IgE decreases ~25% after 1 month and 60% after 2 months; 35% decrease considered good response). Adjunct: azole antifungal (itraconazole used in studies; voriconazole could be used similarly) - IDSA recommends using both steroids and azoles together.

questions.question: Young girl with cystic fibrosis, decline in FEV1 and worsening cough despite antibiotics. Sputum grows Aspergillus.

parts.text: Most likely diagnosis?
Most likely organism (genus and maybe species)?
4 diagnostic criteria
Preferred treatment (1 line)
Additional treatment to consider (1 line)

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely diagnosis: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA).
b) Most likely organism: Aspergillus fumigatus.
c) 4 diagnostic criteria: markedly elevated total IgE (>1000 IU/mL), elevated Aspergillus-specific IgE/positive skin testing, peripheral eosinophilia, and bronchiectasis/infiltrates on imaging.
d) Preferred treatment: oral corticosteroids (prednisone).
e) Additional treatment to consider: itraconazole (steroid-sparing antifungal).

questions.question: A CF patient has a decline in their FEV1. They are given PTZ x 28 days with no improvement. The patient grows a mould in 3 days. There is peripheral eosinophilia.

parts.text: What bug (genus).
b. What syndrome?
c. What 4 diagnostic tests?
d. What preferred treatment and one possible alternate/adjunct?

cohort_answer.text: a) Aspergillus. b) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). c) Aspergillus serum IgE levels; total serum IgE concentration; elevated Aspergillus IgG; Aspergillus positive precipitin test; Aspergillus positive skin test. d) Systemic steroids + itraconazole for 16 weeks (steroids are mainstay; IDSA 2016 recommends concomitant PO itraconazole to reduce antigenic stimulation and be steroid-sparing; ATS 2009 recommends itraconazole only as steroid-sparing or if not responding to steroids alone).

questions.question: CF patient with respiratory symptoms despite therapy for Stenotrophomonas and MRSA. Bronchiectasis. Culture on 4 days of therapy grows chalky white colony NON-branching GPB.

parts.text: What is the next test to identify organism?
b) What is the likely diagnosis?

cohort_answer.text:
Acid fast bacilli smear + culture
Mycobacterium abscessus (tx: Amikacin Imi Clarithro)

questions.question: PM Q25. 5-year old CF patient with recent course of therapy for Steno + MRSA. Still worsening with increased bronchiectasis + alveolar patchy infiltrates. She is otherwise afebrile. She is again started on therapy, and four days in, sputum is growing a gram positive (non-)branching chalky white bacillus.

parts.text: a) What is the most likely pathogen?
b) What is your next step to identify this pathogen?
What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically that can cause a similar clinical picture?

cohort_answer.text:
Most likely pathogen: Mycobacterium abscessus (Nocardia would have filamentous branching though)
Next step: AFB + culture. Nocardia would be weakly acid fast. Tx: Imipenem, amikacin, septra. Others: mero/linezolid

questions.question: Q13 (2013 AM, 2015). CF patient on a drug to treat MRSA and steno in lungs develops worsening resp sx and CT changes. Culture shows non-branching organism, chalky white.

parts.text: A. What is the organism genus and species?
B. What is the next step in determining organism?

cohort_answer.text: A) Possibly B. cepacia complex (often septra resistant; GNB, rod-shaped, motile, obligate aerobic, matte colonial phenotype; treatable with ceftazidime, meropenem, minocycline, TMP/SMX, FQN, aztreonam, imipenem; most resistant to colistin). Alternate answer: Mycobacterium abscessus (may appear refractile GP/GN rods on Gram stain; non-branching distinguishes from Nocardia; grew in 4 days suggesting rapid grower; CF pathogen; wouldn't respond to stenotrophomonas/MRSA therapy; rapid growers <7 days incl abscessus, fortuitum, chelonae). B) MALDI-TOF; specimens may be stained with Ziehl-Neelsen or modification (Kinyoun) and examined by light microscopy.

questions.question:
Q78 (2013 AM)
CF patient with respiratory sx despite tx for stenotrophomonas and MRSA. Bronchiectasis. Culture on 4 days of therapy grows chalky white colony, non-branching GPB.

parts.text: A) What is the next step to identify the organism?

cohort_answer.text: Ziehl-Neilson stain or Kinyoun stain for AFB; MALDI-TOF
